simple: all the programs of a robot, from the ones that drive the motors to the ones that decide where to go, arranged in layers.
analogy: everything in the body that turns seeing into moving: senses, reflexes, balance, thinking.
precise: the set of firmware, operating systems, drivers, middleware and applications of a robot, organised as layers with defined interfaces (messages, rates, units, coordinate frames) and mapped onto the robot's processors; in this course: hardware and safety circuits, microcontroller firmware, the robot computer's OS, middleware, estimation and control, perception and planning, operations.
source: C1 of F9-65 (map, not a source)

simple: how bad it is if a part of the robot fails or is late.
analogy: losing your balance is worse than missing a street sign.
precise: a property of a requirement, decided by hazard analysis, that ranks the consequences of a component's failure; a system is mixed-criticality when components of different criticality share resources such as a processor, memory or a bus, so that a fault in a low-criticality component can interfere with a high-criticality one.

simple: the share of a processor's time that a set of programs needs.
analogy: how much of every second your legs spend pedalling.
precise: for periodic tasks with worst-case execution budgets Ci and periods Ti on one processor, U = Σ Ci/Ti; U > 1 means no scheduler can meet every deadline.

simple: a quick test that says "these tasks surely fit" if the total load is small enough.
analogy: a rule of thumb that you can carry a bag safely if it weighs less than a fixed share of your strength; heavier bags might still be fine, but you must check.
precise: for n independent periodic tasks with deadlines equal to periods under rate-monotonic priorities, U ≤ n(21/n − 1) is sufficient for schedulability (Liu and Layland); it is not necessary. (RB304's F9-46 derives it.)

simple: a calculation of the longest time a task can take from being ready to being done, counting the higher-priority tasks that interrupt it.
analogy: how long a sentence takes when you must stop for every wobble.
precise: for fixed-priority preemptive scheduling, the smallest R with R = Ci + Σj ∈ hp(i) ⌈R/Tj⌉ Cj, found by iteration from R = Ci; the task meets its deadline if R ≤ Di; exact for this task model.

simple: the path a measurement takes through the programs until it moves a motor, and how old the measurement can be when it does.
analogy: from the moment the stone hits the wheel to the moment your hands tighten.
precise: an ordered list of periodic components that pass data forward; with independent periods, each stage can add up to one period of waiting plus its response time, so Σ (Ti + Ri) is a simple upper estimate of the age of the input behind an actuator command (the course's estimate, explained in Layer 3).

simple: a small, separate computer on the robot that runs the fastest motor loops by itself.
analogy: the reflex that tightens your grip before you think.
precise: a microcontroller, usually running bare-metal code or an RTOS, connected to the robot computer by a bus (CAN, UART, SPI, USB or Ethernet), which owns time-critical I/O such as motor current loops and encoder counting and reports to the main computer; curriculum section 17 describes this class of device firmware. (RB304's F9-51 puts micro-ROS on one.)
source: C1 of F9-65 (map, not a source)

simple: a table that counts how often each delay happened.
analogy: counting how many beats were on time, a little late, or very late, over a whole concert.
precise: the distribution of a measured latency over many samples, binned by value, reported with minimum, median, high percentiles (for example p99) and the maximum; for real-time work the tail and the maximum matter more than the mean.

simple: a Linux setting that lets a thread run before all normal threads, until it sleeps or a more important one comes.
analogy: the drummer who plays first, before anyone may speak.
precise: a POSIX real-time scheduling policy in Linux: fixed priorities (1 to 99 on Linux), preemptive, first-in-first-out among threads of equal priority, no time slicing; a SCHED_FIFO thread runs ahead of every SCHED_OTHER (normal) thread on its CPU.

simple: a robot with two kinds of computer: Linux for the rich work, a microcontroller with an RTOS for the fast, strict work.
analogy: the band with two drummers and one rule between them.
precise: a design in which hard-deadline loops run on a separate processor under an RTOS or bare-metal firmware, the application processor runs Linux (often with PREEMPT_RT) for perception, planning, middleware and coordination, and a defined protocol over a bus carries setpoints down and state up, with each side able to reach a safe state if the other stops.
source: C2 of F9-66 (map, not a source)

simple: keeping some processor cores free of everything except the work you choose.
analogy: a practice room where only the drummer may go.
precise: configuring the kernel and the system so that chosen CPUs receive no general tasks, as few interrupts and kernel housekeeping as possible, and only the threads pinned to them; done with kernel boot parameters, interrupt affinity and CPU affinity of threads (the exact parameters are listed, unverified, in Layer 3).

simple: a table that scores each choice against what matters, so the decision can be checked and argued.
analogy: the band's list of what a missed beat costs in each song.
precise: a table of candidate options against weighted criteria; options failing a hard requirement are excluded first, the rest ranked by weighted score, and the ranking is tested for sensitivity to the weights (a choice that flips when one weight changes slightly is not a decision yet).
source: R2 of F9-66 (lab run of this build)

simple: one file that holds everything the robot computer needs to start: the kernel, the description of the board, the settings and the programs.
analogy: the bicycle prepared and packed, with its ticked checklist.
precise: a versioned, reproducibly built artefact (here a GPT disk image) containing the kernel image, the board's devicetree blob, the resolved build configuration, the root file system (in a Linux image), and a manifest of checksums; written to the robot's boot medium or delivered as an update.
source: C1 of F9-67 (map, not a source)

simple: the list of choices made before building the kernel: which drivers and features go in, and with which settings.
analogy: the parts list for the bicycle.
precise: the set of option values (booleans, numbers, strings, "built in" or "module") that selects code and constants at build time; in Linux it is described by Kconfig files (types, defaults, dependencies) and stored as a .config file; in this course's image by mkconfig.py's rules and robot.config. (Kconfig in Zephyr: OS305.)

simple: matching each device described for the board with the program that knows how to drive it.
analogy: giving each cable on the plan to the person who knows that brake.
precise: for devicetree platforms, the kernel walks the nodes, skips those whose status is not "okay", and calls the probe function of the driver whose match table contains one of the node's compatible strings; unmatched nodes stay unbound and are listed. (DR403's F4-35 built a driver model.)

simple: a line of text the loader hands to the kernel at start, with settings that can change without rebuilding.
analogy: a note taped to the handlebar for today's ride.
precise: a string passed by the boot loader, on devicetree systems in the /chosen node's bootargs property, parsed by the kernel and by components that look for their own keys; QEMU's -append option sets it in direct kernel boot.

simple: a list inside the image of every file and its fingerprint, so anyone can check that nothing changed.
analogy: the ticked checklist packed with the toolkit.
precise: a file listing each artefact of the image with a cryptographic hash (here SHA-256), checked before boot or before an update is accepted; it detects corruption, not tampering, unless it is itself signed.

simple: building the same sources twice gives exactly the same bytes.
analogy: the friend builds the identical bicycle from the card.
precise: a build whose output depends only on its declared inputs (sources, configuration, toolchain version), not on time, paths or the machine; verified by building twice and comparing hashes.
source: R3 of F9-67 (lab run of this build)

simple: a note of the time at which each step of starting up finished.
analogy: timing how long until the bicycle is rolling.
precise: a value of a monotonic counter recorded at the end of each start-up stage (here the Arm architectural counter, which counts from reset), printed in the boot log so that boot time can be measured and attributed to stages.

simple: one program of the robot, together with everything needed to start it: where it runs, with which settings, and how it says "I am ready".
analogy: one part of getting on the bicycle (brakes, pedal, look back), each with its own check.
precise: a process (or group of processes, or a container) described by a start command, a target CPU or machine, a configuration (parameters, environment), its dependencies on other units, a readiness signal, and a restart policy; service managers call this a service or a unit, ROS 2 starts nodes through launch files.

simple: "start me after that one has started". It says nothing about whether the other one works.
analogy: sitting down after a foot is on the pedal.
precise: an edge B → A meaning A is launched no earlier than B's process is running; if B never becomes ready, or fails, A is still started. In the lab's format: after=B.
source: R1 of F9-68 (lab run of this build)

simple: "start me only when that one is working, and not at all if it fails".
analogy: do not push off until the brakes have held.
precise: an edge B → A meaning A is launched only after B has reported ready; if B fails, A is blocked, and so is everything that requires A. In the lab's format: needs=B.
source: R1 of F9-68 (lab run of this build)

simple: a message a program sends when it has finished getting ready, which is later than when it started.
analogy: the squeeze on the brake lever that tells you the brakes hold.
precise: an explicit notification from a unit to its supervisor (here the text READY on file descriptor 3) sent after the unit has opened its devices, loaded its parameters and seen its peers; "the process exists" is not readiness.
source: R2 of F9-68 (lab run of this build)

simple: a list of the units in which every unit comes after all the units it waits for.
analogy: the order of getting on the bicycle written as a list.
precise: a linear order of the vertices of a directed acyclic graph consistent with every edge; found by Kahn's algorithm (repeatedly take a vertex with no unprocessed incoming edges); exists if and only if the graph has no cycle.

simple: the chain of units that decides how long start-up takes; making anything else faster does not help.
analogy: the slowest chain of steps between stopping at the kerb and riding away.
precise: the path in the dependency graph, ending at the target unit, along which each unit's launch time was set by its predecessor's running or ready time; its length is the target's ready time.

simple: the rule for what the supervisor does when a unit dies: try again, wait longer each time, and give up after a few tries.
analogy: the chain slips off; you put it back once or twice, but if it keeps coming off you stop riding.
precise: a per-unit specification of whether to restart on failure, the delay (often growing: back-off), the maximum number of attempts in a time window, and the action when the limit is reached (here: stay in the safe state and do not arm).
source: R2 of F9-68 (lab run of this build)

simple: one special unit that becomes ready only when every unit the robot needs to move safely is ready; the robot may be armed only after that.
analogy: the moment you are sitting, feet on pedals, brakes checked.
precise: a target unit (here robot_ready) with requirement dependencies on the safety and motion path; arming is refused until it is ready, and lost if one of its requirements fails later.
source: R1 of F9-68 (lab run of this build)

simple: the condition the robot goes to when something is wrong, chosen so that it cannot hurt anyone while it stays there.
analogy: standing at the side of the road with both feet down.
precise: a defined state of the machine in which the hazard under consideration is absent (for a wheeled robot: stationary, drive disabled, brakes applied where fitted); entered by a safety function and left only by a defined reset; it depends on the hazard: for an arm holding a load, "power off" may drop the load, so the safe state includes holding brakes.

simple: slowing the robot down along a planned ramp first, and only then switching the motors off.
analogy: squeezing the brakes firmly instead of jumping off.
precise: a stop in which the drives remain powered and are commanded to decelerate at a set rate to zero speed, after which power to the drives is removed; contrasted with an uncontrolled stop by immediate removal of power, where the machine coasts or is held by brakes.

simple: a checker that expects a sign of life at regular times and acts when it stops coming.
analogy: the brother who calls and shouts "stop!" when there is no answer.
precise: a monitor with a timeout T that is reset ("kicked", "fed") by the monitored activity; checked every P; detection of a stop happens at most T + P (plus the monitor's own scheduling delay) after the last kick; the action is to request the safe state. A hardware watchdog timer does the same in a counter that resets the processor (HW204).
source: R2 of F9-69 (lab run of this build)

simple: the thing that tells the watchdog "still alive".
analogy: Ama's answer, not the sound of her wheels.
precise: the code path that resets the watchdog; it must be the evidence of useful progress of the monitored function (for example the end of a control cycle that used fresh data), never an independent timer or a thread that runs whatever the function does.
source: R4 of F9-69 (lab run of this build)

simple: once the robot has stopped for a safety reason, it stays stopped even if the reason goes away, until a person resets it.
analogy: the dog has gone, but nobody rides on until someone says "go".
precise: a state that persists after its triggering condition clears; leaving it requires (a) the cause to be gone, (b) the system to be healthy, and (c) a deliberate reset action, and the reset itself must not start motion. (RB101's F9-06 introduced latching.)

simple: the switch, separate from the speed command, that allows a motor drive to make the motor turn at all.
analogy: the chain on the bicycle: without it, pedalling does nothing.
precise: a signal or contactor that permits the power stage of a drive to produce torque; removing it (for example by a safe torque off input of the drive, or a contactor in the motor supply) stops torque regardless of the command value; the e-stop chain acts on this, not on the command.

simple: a short message the robot computer sends to the motor microcontroller many times a second to say it is alive.
analogy: Ama's regular answer to her brother.
precise: a periodic message with a sequence number (often carried with the command stream) from the high-level computer to the real-time controller; the controller enters its safe state when no valid heartbeat arrives within its timeout, so the failure of the whole robot computer is detected by the one component that does not depend on it.
source: C1 of F9-69 (map, not a source)

simple: a small memory that always holds the last few seconds of what the robot's control loop did, so it can be read after something went wrong.
analogy: the cycle computer's recording, but only the last minute, kept forever fresh.
precise: a fixed-size ring buffer of small binary records (time, cycle number, values, event code) written by the real-time code without allocation, locks, system calls or formatting; the oldest records are overwritten; it is dumped to storage on an incident trigger or read after the loop stops. (Lock-free ring buffers: F9-49.)
source: R1 of F9-70 (lab run of this build)

simple: numbers the robot sends while it runs so that people can watch its health from elsewhere.
analogy: the cycle computer sending your speed and heart rate to a friend's phone.
precise: a periodic, usually down-sampled stream of named measurements (rates, temperatures, battery, loop lateness percentiles, counts of faults) sent off the robot over a network to a monitoring system; best effort, never on the control path; distinct from logs (events) and the flight recorder (full-rate, local, recent).
source: C1 of F9-70 (map, not a source)

simple: the list of everything that happened around a problem, in time order, from all the records you have.
analogy: putting the cycle computer's track and the phone's update log side by side.
precise: a merged, time-ordered sequence of observations from logs, traces, recorders and witnesses, each with its source and its clock, used to separate what was observed from what is inferred; requires a common time base or known offsets between clocks.
source: R2 of F9-70 (lab run of this build)

simple: all the records use the same clock, so you can put them in order.
analogy: the cycle computer and the phone both set to the same time.
precise: a clock shared by every record that will be correlated: on one Linux machine the monotonic clock (which never jumps) for intervals and ordering, plus a wall-clock time for matching against the outside world; across machines a synchronised clock with a known error.

simple: a recording, made by the operating system, of which program ran on which CPU and when, and why it stopped.
analogy: a log of who was holding the handlebars at every moment.
precise: a time-stamped stream of kernel events (scheduler switches and wake-ups, interrupts, system calls, driver trace points) recorded into per-CPU buffers by the kernel's tracing infrastructure and read with a tool; it shows which task ran on a CPU while another was waiting.

simple: letting a repeating message through only a few times per second, and counting the rest.
analogy: the friend who says "you're slow" once a minute, not every second.
precise: a limit on how many instances of a message (or of a source) are written per interval, with a count of suppressed instances; protects storage, the CPU and the readability of the log during fault storms, which are exactly the moments that matter.
source: C1 of F9-70 (map, not a source)

simple: one program making another late because they take turns on the same processor.
analogy: the phone update starving the cycle computer app.
precise: the delay a task suffers because another task of equal or higher priority (or a non-preemptible kernel path, or an interrupt handler) runs on the same CPU; removed by placing the time-critical task on a CPU nothing else is allowed to use (CPU isolation and affinity) or by changing priorities.
source: R2 of F9-70 (lab run of this build)

simple: the differences between the simulated robot and the real one that change how the software behaves.
analogy: the living-room trainer versus the gravel road.
precise: the set of unmodelled or mis-modelled effects (delays, friction, saturation, quantisation, noise, parameter errors, compliance, contacts, timing jitter) between a simulation and the physical system, measured by the difference in closed-loop behaviour of the same software under the same scenario.
source: C2 of F9-71 (map, not a source)

simple: how much extra delay a control loop can take before it starts to oscillate without settling.
analogy: how long you can look away from the road before your steering corrections start to make you weave.
precise: for a stable loop with gain crossover frequency ωc and phase margin φm (in radians), the largest added pure time delay that keeps it stable, φm / ωc.

simple: measuring the real robot to find the numbers that the simulator should use.
analogy: timing yourself on the real road to set the trainer's resistance.
precise: estimating the parameters (and sometimes the structure) of a dynamic model from measured inputs and outputs, for example a motor's gain, time constant, dead time and friction from a recorded step response.

simple: testing (or training) in many simulated worlds whose parameters are varied, so that what works does not depend on one exact guess.
analogy: training on the trainer with the resistance changed every few minutes.
precise: sampling the uncertain simulation parameters (delays, friction, masses, sensor noise, calibration) from ranges that cover the real system, and requiring the controller or policy to meet its criteria over the whole range.

simple: running the real robot computer and its real software against a simulated robot body.
analogy: the real bicycle mounted on the trainer.
precise: a test set-up in which the target hardware runs the production software and exchanges real signals (or messages on the real interfaces) with a real-time simulation of the plant; contrasted with software-in-the-loop (SIL), where the production software runs on a development computer against the simulator.
source: C2 of F9-71 (map, not a source)

simple: a number in the software that describes the real hardware, such as how many encoder counts make one turn or how big the wheel is.
analogy: the wheel size set in the bicycle computer.
precise: a constant in the measurement or actuation path (encoder counts per revolution, gear ratio, wheel radius, sensor offset and scale) that converts between raw hardware units and physical units; an error in it scales or offsets every measurement, and a feedback loop closed on that measurement faithfully tracks the wrong quantity.
source: R2 of F9-71 (lab run of this build)

simple: an encoder counts whole steps, so speed computed from counts jumps in fixed steps.
analogy: counting fence posts to guess your speed.
precise: speed estimated as Δcount × 2π / (CPR × Δt) can only take multiples of 2π / (CPR × Δt); with 1024 counts per revolution and Δt = 1 ms, that step is 6.14 rad/s.
source: R2 of F9-71 (lab run of this build)
